text: Every login and permission from Chapter 4 assumes the connection already reached SQL Server. The firewall is the layer before that — it checks the source IP first, and rejects the packet before login is even attempted.
A server-level firewall rule applies to every database on the logical server — a name, a start IP, and an end IP. Anything outside that range never gets far enough to try a password.
The server's Networking page holds every firewall rule, the public network access toggle, and one setting that trips people up — "Allow Azure services and resources to access this server."

Server-level rules cover the whole server. Database-level rules scope one database. The Azure-services checkbox doesn't allow one resource — it opens the door to any Azure resource in any subscription that also passes login.
Get the firewall wrong and no correctly-scoped permission downstream fixes it. Next up: Virtual Networks and service endpoints, a tighter control than an IP allow-list.
